transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well… I’m here because people keep telling me I’m imagining things, or that I’m “reading into it,” but I know what I’ve seen. The hospital people, and some people from the agency I work through, they’ve been watching our house and even the cleaning routes I take. It’s like they’re checking up on me, seeing if I’m taking proper care of my husband, like they don’t trust me to do it right.

And it’s not just a feeling, you know? It’s little things—the way people act, the timing of things, how they seem to know where I’ve been. I clean houses, so I’m out on different routes, and I notice when someone is paying attention. I’ve done this work a long time. I’m not stupid. But when I try to explain it, people look at me like I’m making it up, and that’s why I came in, because I need somebody to actually listen instead of just brushing me off.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

Yes… I mean, I do hear a voice sometimes, but it’s not like how people make it sound. It’s not constant, and I’m not just sitting there making it up. It usually happens when the house is quiet, like when everything has settled down and I’m near the kitchen. I’ll hear a woman’s voice by the kitchen window, very clear, like she’s standing right there outside or just close enough that I should be able to see her.

She’ll say things like I need to check the locks, or that I should move my husband’s pills. And I know how that sounds, but it doesn’t feel like a thought in my own head. It sounds like someone speaking to me, plain as anything. I’ll look, and no one is there, but I still heard it. So yes, I guess the answer is yes.
Have you had a time when you felt unusually high or energized for days at a time?

Yes… yes, I have times like that. It’s not like I’m trying to be difficult or anything, but I’ll get up before it’s even daylight, before most people are thinking about moving, and I’m already cleaning, getting things straightened, starting food, checking what needs to be done.

And then one thing turns into another. I’ll be making lists, then making another list because the first one wasn’t organized right, then I’m calling about appointments or trying to set things up, and before you know it I’ve taken on church errands too—like someone needs something dropped off, or there’s a call to make, or something to organize, and I’ll say, “I can do it,” even if my family is telling me I need to sit down and slow myself.

But at the time it doesn’t feel wrong to me. It feels like there’s finally enough energy to get everything handled, like if I don’t do it right then and there, it’ll all fall apart or get missed. Other people will say I’m doing too much, but I feel like I’m just trying to stay on top of things.
When you hear that woman’s voice by the kitchen window, does it happen only during those times when you feel unusually energized?

No… no, it isn’t only when I’m wound up like that. I know why you’re asking, because I do have those stretches where I’m up early and doing too much, but there was a quieter time too—several weeks, I’d say—where I wasn’t rushing around the same way.

I was sleeping more then, and I wasn’t taking on so much or moving so fast. My family probably would’ve said I was calmer, or at least not constantly trying to get everything done at once. But even during that time, I still heard that woman’s voice by the kitchen window. And I still had that feeling—well, more than a feeling to me—that the agency people were watching us, checking on the house and whether I was handling things right.

So no, it doesn’t just happen when I have all that energy. It can happen even when I’m slowed down.
Have the voice and the sense that people are watching you been going on for longer than a month?

Yes… it’s definitely been longer than a month. I wish I could say it was just a short spell, like a bad week or something, but it’s been going on for quite a while now.

If I think back on it, the voice and that feeling like people are watching us or checking on us… it’s been about eleven months. Not every single minute of every day, but it keeps coming back, and it’s been part of my life for most of this past year. It’s hard to admit that out loud, because when you say “eleven months” it sounds so much bigger than when you’re just trying to get through each day.
Have you been diagnosed with any brain or nervous system illness?

No… not that I know of. I mean, nobody has ever sat me down and told me I have some brain illness or nerve disease or anything like that.

I’ve had regular aches and tiredness like people get, and I’ve been to doctors for ordinary things over the years, but as far as something with my brain or nervous system… I don’t have a diagnosis like that. If there was something in my chart, nobody explained it to me that way.
Since these problems began, have you been less able to do your work or take care of things at home than you were before?

Yes… yes, I have. I don’t like saying that, because I’ve always been someone who worked hard, especially with cleaning. I knew my routes, I knew what clients liked, and I used to be the person they trusted to keep things moving.

But since all this started, the agency took away my supervisory routes. They didn’t just say it out of nowhere—there were complaints, I guess, from clients and coworkers saying they couldn’t rely on my work the way they used to. That hurt a lot. I tried to explain that I was still trying, but it’s like things were slipping, and people noticed before I wanted to admit it.

And at home, too… my husband has had to step in more. My pastor too, actually. Not just for emotional support, but with real things—making sure the caregiving and household responsibilities are handled safely, because I haven’t been keeping up like before. I used to manage so much of that myself, and now it feels like other people are having to watch over the things I should be handling. It’s embarrassing, but yes, I’m less able than I was.
During this past year, have you had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

I’m not really sure how to answer that exactly. I mean… I’ve had times where I’ve felt really worn down and upset, and some days I just don’t feel like myself, but if you’re asking whether there was a clear two-week stretch where I was depressed most of the day nearly every day… I don’t know that I can say that for sure.

I don’t want to say yes if I’m not remembering it right. Sometimes everything kind of blends together when you’re just trying to keep going day by day. There have been bad days, definitely, but I’m not sure I noticed it in that kind of steady, every-day-for-two-weeks way.
Was there ever a time when the voice and the feeling of being watched lasted for at least two weeks when you were not feeling unusually energized or depressed?

Yes… I think there was. I’m trying to place it right, because I don’t want to make it sound more exact than it was, but there was a quieter spell for several weeks where I wasn’t all keyed up like before. I was sleeping more then, and I wasn’t rushing around so much or acting like I had to get everything done right that second.

But even during that calmer time, I still heard the voice by the kitchen window. And I still had that feeling that the agency was watching us. It didn’t go away just because I wasn’t as energized. I also don’t think I was deeply depressed then, not like lying there crying all day or anything like that. It was more like things had slowed down, but the watching feeling and the voice were still there in the background… sometimes not even background, honestly. It still felt real to me.
During those high-energy periods, did you need much less sleep than usual and still feel rested?

Yes… that definitely happened. During those times, I could sleep maybe two or three hours, and then I’d wake up like I’d had a full night. Not groggy, not dragging myself around like I normally would if I slept that little.

I’d get up and feel ready to do things right away—like scrub the floors, sort through papers, start cleaning things that didn’t even need to be cleaned at that hour. It wasn’t like when you can’t sleep and you feel miserable the next day. I felt awake, like my body didn’t need the rest. That’s part of what made it hard for me to see it as a problem at first, because I thought, well, at least I’m getting things done. But yes, I needed a lot less sleep and still felt rested.
During those high-energy times, did you find yourself talking much more than usual?

I’m not completely sure about that one. I mean, I know I was more wound up inside during those times, and I probably had more to say just because my mind felt busy, but I don’t know if I was talking much more than usual in a way other people would have noticed.

Sometimes I’m talkative anyway if I’m upset or if I feel like I need to explain myself, and other times I keep things in. So it’s hard for me to separate what was really different from just… me trying to get my thoughts out. I don’t remember anyone specifically saying, “You’re talking too much,” or anything like that. Maybe I talked faster or went on longer than I realized, but I can’t say for sure.
During those high-energy times, did you feel especially powerful, important, or as if you had special abilities that other people didn’t?

Yes… I did, though I don’t know if I would have called it “powerful” at the time. It felt more like I had to be the one to handle things, because nobody else was really seeing it clearly enough.

I remember feeling like I was the only one with enough sense and strength to keep my husband safe, and to keep the house safe, and even some of the people from church. Like I had a responsibility on me that other people didn’t understand. It wasn’t just, “Oh, I’m better than everyone.” It was more like… I believed I had something in me, some kind of ability to notice what was coming and stand up to it when other people couldn’t.

And I know that sounds like a lot when I say it out loud now, but at the time it felt very serious. I felt important in that way, like if I didn’t stay on top of things, something bad could happen and it would be because I failed to protect everyone.
At any time during this past year, did you have a period when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks?

I’m not really sure how to answer that. I mean, I’ve had times where I felt really low, and I can get worn down, but “most of the day nearly every day for two weeks” is hard for me to pin down.

I don’t keep track of it like that, you know? Some days feel heavy, and then other days I can still get up and do what I need to do, even if I don’t feel great. So I don’t want to say yes if I’m not sure it was that steady or that long. It may have happened, but I honestly can’t clearly say, “Yes, it was every day like that for two weeks.”
During those high-energy times, did you find yourself starting a lot more projects or activities than usual?

Yes, I think so. That part I can say more clearly. When I get like that, I don’t just sit around feeling energized — I start doing things, a lot of things, and usually too early.

I’ll be up before daylight, before anybody really needs to be moving, and I’ll already be cleaning something or cooking, like starting food when it’s not even time yet, wiping counters, sorting things, making piles, deciding the whole house needs to be straightened right then. And then I’ll start making lists — not just one list, but new lists because I think of something else, appointments I need to call about, things that need to be checked on, errands, what needs to be done for the house.

And I’d take on extra things from church too, like errands or helping with something, even when people would say, “You need to slow down,” or “That can wait.” But in my mind it couldn’t wait. It felt like if I had the energy and I could see what needed doing, then I should just do it. So yes, I was starting more things and putting more on myself than usual.
Did any of those high-energy periods last at least a week?

Yes, I think some of them did. It wasn’t just like one busy day and then I was back to normal the next morning.

The hard part is that it’s been kind of on and off, so I don’t always have a clean start and stop date in my head. But these stretches where I’m really keyed up, more irritable, and barely sleeping have been happening for… I’d say around ten months now, off and on. And yes, within that, there have been times where it lasted at least a week, not just a couple days. It would keep going enough that people around me could tell it wasn’t just normal energy.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think there was. I’m trying to place it right, because I don’t want to make it sound more exact than it was, but there was a quieter spell for several weeks where I wasn’t all keyed up like before. I was sleeping more then, and I wasn’t rushing around so much or acting like I had to get everything done right that second.

But even during that calmer time, I still heard the voice by the kitchen window. And I still had that feeling that the agency was watching us. It didn’t go away just because I wasn’t as energized. I also don’t think I was deeply depressed then, not like lying there crying all day or anything like that. It was more like things had slowed down, but the watching feeling and the voice were still there in the background… sometimes not even background, honestly. It still felt real to me.

inference.note: Updated F25.9 to F25.0 because there is a clear manic syndrome and at least 2 weeks of hallucinations/persecutory delusions outside of mood episodes, supporting schizoaffective disorder, manic type. F20.0 remains as a differential given persistent delusions/auditory hallucinations with functional decline >6 months.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated periods meet a core manic criterion by involving decreased need for sleep, helping distinguish schizoaffective disorder from schizophrenia with nonspecific activation.
doctor.question: During those high-energy periods, did you need much less sleep than usual and still feel rested?

target_item.name: Decreased_Sleep
target_item.manifestation: Many nights I sleep two or three hours and wake up ready to scrub floors or sort papers, not tired like I used to be after a short night.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether, during high-energy periods, the patient needed much less sleep than usual and still felt rested.

patient.answer:
Yes… that definitely happened. During those times, I could sleep maybe two or three hours, and then I’d wake up like I’d had a full night. Not groggy, not dragging myself around like I normally would if I slept that little.

I’d get up and feel ready to do things right away—like scrub the floors, sort through papers, start cleaning things that didn’t even need to be cleaned at that hour. It wasn’t like when you can’t sleep and you feel miserable the next day. I felt awake, like my body didn’t need the rest. That’s part of what made it hard for me to see it as a problem at first, because I thought, well, at least I’m getting things done. But yes, I needed a lot less sleep and still felt rested.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated periods included abnormally increased talkativeness/pressured speech, to clarify whether the patient has had a full manic episode supporting schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, versus schizophrenia.
doctor.question: During those high-energy times, did you find yourself talking much more than usual?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about being much more talkative than usual during high-energy periods, but the provided symptom profile does not include a distinct item for increased talkativeness or pressured speech. The closest speech-related item is disorganized thinking/speech, which is about scattered or hard-to-follow speech rather than talking more than usual.

patient.answer:
I’m not completely sure about that one. I mean, I know I was more wound up inside during those times, and I probably had more to say just because my mind felt busy, but I don’t know if I was talking much more than usual in a way other people would have noticed.

Sometimes I’m talkative anyway if I’m upset or if I feel like I need to explain myself, and other times I keep things in. So it’s hard for me to separate what was really different from just… me trying to get my thoughts out. I don’t remember anyone specifically saying, “You’re talking too much,” or anything like that. Maybe I talked faster or went on longer than I realized, but I can’t say for sure.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated-energy episodes included grandiosity, which would help confirm a true manic syndrome and distinguish schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, from schizophrenia.
doctor.question: During those high-energy times, did you feel especially powerful, important, or as if you had special abilities that other people didn’t?

target_item.name: Inflated_Self_Esteem
target_item.manifestation: I started feeling like I was the only one with the sense and strength to keep my husband, my home, and even some of the church people safe from what was coming.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether, during high-energy periods, the patient felt especially powerful, important, or had special abilities, which directly matches inflated self-esteem or grandiosity.

patient.answer:
Yes… I did, though I don’t know if I would have called it “powerful” at the time. It felt more like I had to be the one to handle things, because nobody else was really seeing it clearly enough.

I remember feeling like I was the only one with enough sense and strength to keep my husband safe, and to keep the house safe, and even some of the people from church. Like I had a responsibility on me that other people didn’t understand. It wasn’t just, “Oh, I’m better than everyone.” It was more like… I believed I had something in me, some kind of ability to notice what was coming and stand up to it when other people couldn’t.

And I know that sounds like a lot when I say it out loud now, but at the time it felt very serious. I felt important in that way, like if I didn’t stay on top of things, something bad could happen and it would be because I failed to protect everyone.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a full major depressive episode during the illness, which would favor schizoaffective disorder over paranoid schizophrenia.
doctor.question: At any time during this past year, did you have a period when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a major depressive episode, specifically depressed mood most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks. The provided symptom profile does not include depressive mood symptoms, so no listed item directly covers this.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure how to answer that. I mean, I’ve had times where I felt really low, and I can get worn down, but “most of the day nearly every day for two weeks” is hard for me to pin down.

I don’t keep track of it like that, you know? Some days feel heavy, and then other days I can still get up and do what I need to do, even if I don’t feel great. So I don’t want to say yes if I’m not sure it was that steady or that long. It may have happened, but I honestly can’t clearly say, “Yes, it was every day like that for two weeks.”

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated periods included increased goal-directed activity, a key manic symptom that would support schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type over schizophrenia.
doctor.question: During those high-energy times, did you find yourself starting a lot more projects or activities than usual?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I get moving before daylight, cleaning, cooking, calling about appointments, making new lists, and taking on church errands even when everyone tells me to slow down.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether, during high-energy periods, the patient started more projects or activities than usual, which directly reflects increased goal-directed activity or energy.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think so. That part I can say more clearly. When I get like that, I don’t just sit around feeling energized — I start doing things, a lot of things, and usually too early.

I’ll be up before daylight, before anybody really needs to be moving, and I’ll already be cleaning something or cooking, like starting food when it’s not even time yet, wiping counters, sorting things, making piles, deciding the whole house needs to be straightened right then. And then I’ll start making lists — not just one list, but new lists because I think of something else, appointments I need to call about, things that need to be checked on, errands, what needs to be done for the house.

And I’d take on extra things from church too, like errands or helping with something, even when people would say, “You need to slow down,” or “That can wait.” But in my mind it couldn’t wait. It felt like if I had the energy and I could see what needed doing, then I should just do it. So yes, I was starting more things and putting more on myself than usual.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a full manic episode lasting at least one week, which would favor schizoaffective disorder over schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Did any of those high-energy periods last at least a week?

target_item.name: Manic Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The stretches of being unusually energized, irritable, and barely sleeping have been happening on and off for about 10 months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of high-energy/manic periods, specifically whether they lasted at least a week.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think some of them did. It wasn’t just like one busy day and then I was back to normal the next morning.

The hard part is that it’s been kind of on and off, so I don’t always have a clean start and stop date in my head. But these stretches where I’m really keyed up, more irritable, and barely sleeping have been happening for… I’d say around ten months now, off and on. And yes, within that, there have been times where it lasted at least a week, not just a couple days. It would keep going enough that people around me could tell it wasn’t just normal energy.

inference.note: Psychosis has persisted for at least 2 weeks outside mood episodes, ruling out F20.0 in favor of schizoaffective disorder, manic type. There is clear evidence of mania (decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, inflated sense of special role/importance, episodes lasting at least a week) plus psychotic symptoms over ~11 months with functional decline.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has persistent psychotic symptoms for about 11 months, including auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions, along with clear manic episodes marked by decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, and grandiose/responsibility-based beliefs lasting at least a week. Crucially, psychotic symptoms also persisted for at least two weeks during a period without mania or depression, which supports schizoaffective disorder, manic type, over bipolar disorder with psychotic symptoms. Schizophrenia was considered, but the presence of prominent syndromal mania makes schizoaffective disorder more fitting.
